items.stem: A distant galaxy's spectral lines are shifted toward longer (redder) wavelengths. This indicates that the galaxy is

options.text: receding from us, consistent with an expanding universe
options.rationale: Correct: cosmological redshift indicates recession in an expanding universe.

options.text: made of different elements than the Sun
options.rationale: The shift is in wavelength of known lines, not composition.
Temperature alone does not shift line wavelengths this way.

items.explanation: Correct: cosmological redshift indicates recession in an expanding universe.
items.provenance: original Mastemy item drafted by an AI agent; no external question source

items.stem: Which TWO observations are considered strong evidence for the Big Bang model? (Select TWO.)

options.rationale: Correct: the CMB is relic radiation predicted by the Big Bang.

options.text: The observed abundances of light elements such as hydrogen and helium
options.rationale: Correct: primordial nucleosynthesis predicts these abundances.

options.text: The existence of black holes at galaxy centres
options.rationale: Supermassive black holes are not primary Big Bang evidence.

options.text: The constancy of the speed of light
options.rationale: That is a relativity postulate, not Big Bang evidence.

items.explanation: Correct: the CMB is relic radiation predicted by the Big Bang.

items.stem: Flat rotation curves of spiral galaxies, where outer stars orbit as fast as inner ones, are evidence for

options.text: additional unseen mass, attributed to dark matter
options.rationale: Correct: visible mass cannot explain the flat curves, implying dark matter.

options.text: the galaxies being much smaller than they appear
options.rationale: Size estimates do not resolve the rotation-curve discrepancy.

options.text: a failure of the Doppler effect
options.rationale: The Doppler effect is well established and used to measure the curves.
Expansion governs large-scale recession, not internal galaxy rotation.
